3 It is worthwhile to mention that after considering the final arguments as well as material available on record, the Ld. Trial Court passed the impugned judgment and order dated 30.11.2019, which is reproduced as under:-
"7.1. Khasra no.108 Village Jafrabad is now owned by the Govt. as it had been acquired and compensation paid (vide award no.2058).
The said acquisition was permanent (vide document Ex.PW2/1).
7.2. Thus this court is cognizant of the title to the land on which the suit property is situated.
Any occupier of the said land other than the Union of India is a squatter and this suit can not be decided therefore on better title as the perfect title is known.
No squatter can claim possession from another squatter.
8. It is found that the plaintiff can not seek eviction of any person from the suit property for the reason above discussed.
9. Given the finding on issue no.1 to 3 no party to the present suit is entitled to any relief."

4 Aggrieved by the said judgment and order dated 30.11.2019, the appellants preferred the present appeal mainly on the grounds that:-
a) Because the Ld. Trial Court erred in failing to consider that law laid down in Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013, wherein section 24 (2) of the 2013 Act categorically provides that if in land acquisition proceedings wherein an award has been passed five years prior to the new Act but the possession has not been taken by the land acquiring authority the acquisition stands lapsed.

sentences.text: Ld. Trial Court has erroneously held that the land acquired by the Govt. is even at the date of passing judgment belongs to government and any occupier other than government i.e. Union of India is a squatter.
The said reason is a primary reason to dismiss the suit and the same is fundamentally wrong in the light of the statutory mandate which clearly considers the proceedings to be lapsed.

Section relied upon is reproduced herein below for the ready reference of the court:-
"Section 24: Land acquisition process under Act No.1 of 1894 shall be deemed to have lapsed in certain case:-

2 1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, in any case of land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894-- a) Where no award under section 11 of the said Land Acquisition Act has been made,
then, all provisions of this Act relating to the determination of compensation shall apply; or b) Where an award under said section 11 has been made, then such proceedings shall continue under the provisions of the said Land Acquisition Act, as if the said Act has not been repealed.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), in case of land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (1 of 1894), where an award under the said section 11 has been made five years or more prior to the commencement of this Act but the physical possession of the land has not been taken or the compensation has not been paid the said proceedings shall be deemed to have lapsed and the appropriate government, if it so chooses, shall initiate the proceedings of such land acquisition afresh in accordance with the provisions of this Act:
Provided that where an award has been made and compensation in respect of a majority of land holdings has not been deposited in the account of the beneficiaries,
then all beneficiaries specified in the notification for acquisition under section 4 of the said Land Acquisition Act, shall be entitled to compensation in accordance with the provisions of this Act."
b) Because, the Ld. Trial Court erred in failing to consider that both the parties in the suit had claimed ownership and despite that the Ld. Trial Court failed to frame the issue regarding the ownership of the suit property.

c) Because the Ld. Trial Court erred in failing to consider the law clarified by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that in a case where both the parties are claiming ownership over a property and wherein one of the party is alleged to be a tenant and the party discharging its burden to prove the ownership should be considered as an owner of the property and accordingly the issue must be decided.
d) Because the Ld. Trial court erred in failing to consider that the appellants had produced documents evidence to prove the ownership and the rent agreement between the parties over the suit property and whereas the defendant who claimed to be the owner of the suit property did not produce a single document to prove his ownership.
e) Because the Ld. Trial court erred in failing to consider that unregistered documents can be admissible in evidence for proving title of a disputed property.

Trial court erred in failing to consider that by producing the documentary evidence in their favour and of the chain owners i.e. the GPA, SPA and the Agreement to Sell being registered and notarized, the appellants had discharged their burden/onus to prove the ownership over the suit property.
g) Because the impugned judgment is not a well- reasoned judgment and does not cover the relevant aspects of the subject suit.
The judgment itself shows that the Ld. Trial court has not looked into the evidence of the parties and the truth extracted from the parties during the cross examination.

h) Because the Ld. Trial Court erred in failing to appreciate the cross examination of the defendants witness which shows nothing but glaring contradictions and presents the truth that all of the witnesses were deposing falsely before the Ld. Trial Court.

i) Because the Ld. Trial Court erred in failing to consider the statement of DW-4 where he states that Shop No.1, 2 and 4 of in House No.1 belongs to the appellant and further admitted that deceased defendant came in possession of the shop some 14-15 years ago, whereas DW1 states that he came in possession only in 2014.

j) Because the Ld. Trial Court erred in failing to consider the statement of DW5 where he states that he met the appellant for sale of the said shop alongwith the defendant no.1 in 2004, whereas the DW1 on the contrary stated that in the sale of the shop took place in 2014.

Further, he admits that the said sale document prepared contained the signature of the deceased defendant whereas DW1 stated that the deceased defendant was illiterate and used to affix his thumb impression.
k) Because the Ld. Trial Court erred in failing to appreciate the law of evidence which requires that documentary evidence must be given higher weightage compared to oral testimonies.
That the appellants had produced the documentary evidence to show the existence of tenancy.
The same was disputed by the defendant on the ground that the defendant was illiterate and did not sign.

That Ld.
Trial Court failed to appreciate the evidence of DW5 wherein he states that he is illiterate but knows how to write his name.
It is pertinent to note that DW5 being an illiterate have signed his name on his statement.

5 Perusal of the grounds upon which the present appeal has been preferred clearly reveals that the main grievance of the appellant admittedly is that Ld. Trial Court did not appreciate the evidence of the parties and passed the impugned judgment on the ground that suit property which is situated in Khasra No.108, Village Jafrabad has been acquired by the government for which compensation has been paid vide award no.2058.

sentences.text:
The parties to an appeal shall not be entitled to produce additional evidence,
whether oral or documentary, in the Appellate Court.

But if (a) the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has refused to admit evidence which ought to have been admitted, or [(aa) the party seeking to produce additional evidence, establishes that notwithstanding the exercise of due diligence, such evidence was not within his knowledge or could not, after the exercise of due diligence, be produced by him at the time when the decree appealed against was passed, or]

(b) the Appellate Court requires any document to be produced or any witness to be examined to enable it to pronounce judgment, or for any other substantial cause, the Appellate Court may allow such evidence or document to be produced, or witness to be examined.
2) Whenever additional evidence is allowed to be produced by an Appellate court, the court shall record the reason for its admission.

15 In the suit filed by the plaintiffs, the plaintiffs and defendant both had claimed ownership qua suit property, but a perusal of impugned judgment Ld. Trial Court did not give any findings on this fact.

Patwari.

16 A perusal of 27 Rule of Order 41 CPC goes to show that rule (aa) has been inserted by Code of Civil procedure (amendment) Act 1976 with a view to provide that additional evidence may be received by the appellate court if the appellant satisfies the court that after the exercise of due diligence such evidence was not in his knowledge or could not be produced when the matter was decided against him.

17 The law is well-settled that the Appellate Court has unbridled powers to order re-trial or direct recording of additional evidence if it is satisfied that the additional evidence is essential to promote Mohd. sentences.text: The courts do not exist merely for disposal of cases but are established for dispensing justice.

18 In Billa Jagan Mohan Reddy and Anr. v. Billa Sanjeeva Reddy and Ors.; 1994 (4) SCC 659, it was held by their lordships of the Supreme Court that if the documents are found to be relevant to decide the real issue in controversy and when the court felt that interest of justice requires that the documents may be received, exercising the power under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC, the appellate court would receive the documents and consider their effect thereof.

entities.text: Billa Jagan Mohan Reddy and Anr. v. Billa Sanjeeva Reddy and Ors.; 1994 (4) SCC 659
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was further held in the said authority that when such is the position, when the documents are sought to be produced in the trial court, before the arguments are completed, normally they may be received; an opportunity given to prove them and rebuttal if any and their relevance and effect they may have, be considered in deciding the issues arising in the Controversy.

It was further held that under those circumstances,
the court was not justified in refusing to receive the document and the High Court also committed the same error in not considering the effect in this behalf in the right perspective.

19 Further, in "Rajeshwar Prasad Mishra Vs. State of West Bengal & Anr.; AIR 1965 SC 1887", Hon'ble Apex Court observed that the Code gives power to the Appellate Court for taking additional evidence.

entities.text: Rajeshwar Prasad Mishra Vs. State of West Bengal & Anr.; AIR 1965 SC 1887
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Additional evidence must be necessary not because it would be impossible to pronounce the judgment, but because there would be failure of justice without it.
The power, however, has to be exercised sparingly and only in suitable cases.
Once such action is justified, there is no restriction on the kind of evidence which may be received.
20 Thus, in view of aforesaid authoritative pronouncements, it becomes clear that court has unbridled power to permit additional evidence.
Only rider is that it should not be made to fill up the lacuna, rather it should be relevant for just decision of the case.

21 I may observe that in so far as the provisions of Order 41 Rule 27 CPC are concerned, the general rule is that ordinarily the appellant court cannot traverse beyond the record of Trial Court and admit the additional evidence on mere asking but Section 107 CPC is an exception to this rule and said evidence can be taken on record as permissible under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC.

In the present case the additional evidence which the appellants now seek to bring on record as aforesaid i.e. copy of the possession proceedings report arising out of the award no.2058 (Annexure A1) and copy of Compensation determination proceedings for the same (Annexure A2).

Since the award no.2058 has no award in the eyes of law and since possession of Khasra No.108 was never taken by the Land Acquisition Collector in respect to award no.2058, therefore, this court is of the opinion that documents i.e. copy of the possession proceedings report arising out of the award no.2058 (Annexure A1) and copy of Compensation determination proceedings for the same (Annexure A2) are very much necessary and relevant documents for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties.

Trial Court dated 30.11.2019 is set aside and the case is remanded back with the directions to the Ld. Trial Court to grant two effective opportunities to the appellant to lead evidence to prove the above said documents i.e. copy of the possession proceedings report arising out of the award no.2058 (Annexure A1) and copy of Compensation determination proceedings for the same (Annexure A2) which shall be subject to right to rebuttal by the respondent after which Ld.
Trial Court shall render fresh findings on the issues in accordance with law.
